title: Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela
summary: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela in northern Ethiopia are monolithic and cave churches cut into volcanic tuff around 1200 CE under King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty, who is said to have planned a new Jerusalem. Bete Giyorgis, a cross-shaped church sunk in its own trench, is the best known. The churches are still in use.

uncertainty.note: The churches are thought to have been cut within a 100-year period around 1200 AD (ISPRS), and UNESCO attributes the work to the 12th century; start is 1150 with that spread. End is the present: the churches are in use.

footprint.description: Cross-shaped monolithic church 12 by 12 m in plan standing in a square trench about 25 m on a side, cut free from volcanic tuff (ISPRS photogrammetric article, University of Melbourne). Bete Giyorgis stands apart from the two main church groups. No survey polygon was opened.

reviewer_note: Shape block, modelling only Bete Giyorgis (the place record covers the whole site). The construction window 1150-1250 follows 'a 100-year period around 1200 AD' and is approximate. Trench depth was not found in a university or museum source, so none is stored. The UNESCO XML point for property 18 (12.0333 N, 38.8167 E) puts the longitude about 24 km west of the town, so the OpenStreetMap node for Bete Giorgis is used instead.
